transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-03-25 15:30 PST | Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE); Priya Patel (Redwood SE); Michael Ross (NovaHealth CTO); Sara Li (ML Platform Lead); Daniel Kim (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Deep dive into throughput tuning for NovaHealth's conversational workloads.
- Discussed continuous batching behavior, scheduler knobs (max_batch_latency_ms, max_batch_size), and max_num_seqs for sequence packing.
- KV cache warmup and shard locality identified as key for 99th percentile latency.
- Quantization tradeoffs: int8 gains but watch for QA/regression on rare tokens; suggested A/B on Dedicated pools.
- Next steps: Redwood share tuning playbook, NovaHealth to run benchmark in staging VPC.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, really appreciate you making time. We'll dig into throughput tuning for the NovaHealth conversational routing workload. Priya and I will run through knobs and then we can get into specifics, please interrupt.
[00:14] Michael Ross: Great, thanks Alex. Quick context, we are trying to push to real-time chat for triage flows, 95th pct target under 300ms for short queries but we're seeing 500 to 1k at times on the staging cluster.
[00:26] Priya Patel: Okay thanks Mike, yeah so first thing I wanna understand is your current traffic shape — mean tokens per request, percent long sequences, do you have a lot of short and a few very long ones?
[00:36] Sara Li: Roughly 70% are short, 20% medium (50-150 tokens), and 10% long (200-600 tokens). We also have a daily burst around 9am with spikes to 3x baseline.
[00:49] Daniel Kim: We're on EKS, VPC peered into our prod account, and currently running with a single shared pool of g4dn-style instances — not ideal, we know. We also have KMS in the same VPC for keys.
[01:02] Priya Patel: Good, that helps. So with that distribution you get a lot of small sequences which are ideal for continuous batching but the scheduler knobs matter. The key knobs to tune are: max_batch_size, max_batch_latency_ms, and max_num_seqs.
[01:18] Alex Chen: I'll add token limits and sequence packing. For example, if you allow sequence packing with max_num_seqs=8 you'll fill batches more effectively but watch out for memory and KV cache thrash on long sequences.
[01:33] Michael Ross: Can you explain the trade-off between max_batch_latency_ms and user-perceived latency? If we increase latency wait time to fill batches, doesn't that hurt the 95th pct?
[01:44] Priya Patel: Yeah so it's a trade. If you set max_batch_latency_ms to say 20ms you'll wait up to 20ms to try and group requests into a batch — that increases tail a little for individual requests that miss a batch, but it significantly improves throughput and lowers cost-per-token. For NovaHealth, with 70% short requests, starting at 10-25ms usually gives a good sweet spot.
[02:05] Daniel Kim: What about max_batch_size? We saw some config default at 64 which seemed arbitrarily high and caused GPU mem pressure.
[02:12] Priya Patel: Yup default numbers are conservative. For your instance types and model (you said 7B? or 13B?), what are you running?
[02:19] Michael Ross: We're currently on an open 13B variant quantized to int8 in staging.
[02:24] Priya Patel: Okay 13B int8 — memory footprint lower but kernel selection and memory fragmentation matter. For 13B I'd recommend max_batch_size 16-32 depending on sequence length. With many short sequences sequence packing (max_num_seqs) into the same batch recovers more throughput than brute forcing a large max_batch_size.
[02:42] Alex Chen: Also watch per-request token_limit. If clients are sending very generous max_tokens it can generate long sequences unexpectedly. Set server-side per-route token caps.
[02:51] Sara Li: We do have a few customers using long-form generation, can we set per-route limits?
[02:56] Priya Patel: Absolutely, you can set per-route token caps and fallback policies. You can also have a separate Dedicated pool for long-running generation so it doesn't affect short-chat latency.
[03:07] Michael Ross: We heard something about max_num_seqs causing sequence packing to mis-order requests or increase latency for some requests — any truth to that?
[03:14] Priya Patel: There's some nuance — packing merges multiple user sequences into a single multi-sequence batch so you need deterministic padding and careful KV cache accounting. It won't re-order requests in terms of completion, but if a long sequence is packed with short ones you might see variance. The scheduler supports affinity knobs so you can bias packing away from mixing long and short sequences.
[03:34] Daniel Kim: Okay that makes sense. What about KV cache warmup? Right now our 95th pct spikes on the first few requests after a pod spin-up.
[03:42] Priya Patel: That's a classic. The KV cache is populated as tokens are generated; cold starts will pay the cost of cache warmup. For high-availability you can:
- keep a small warm pool of pods that are pre-warmed with common prefixes
- use prefix caching for the most common prompts
- reduce scale-to-zero aggressiveness during expected windows
[03:57] Alex Chen: And on Dedicated we can keep KV shard affinity so repeat users hit the same shard which reduces cross-shard misses.
[04:05] Michael Ross: You mentioned prefix caching — can you give an example?
[04:09] Priya Patel: Sure. If 80% of requests start with the triage system prompt you can precompute that prefix KV state and reuse it as the base for incoming requests instead of re-encoding every time. That drops per-request compute significantly.
[04:20] Sara Li: How does this interact with quantization, any regressions we should watch for?
[04:25] Priya Patel: Quantization to int8 or 4-bit can change logits at rare tokens; for chat triage it's usually fine but you should run evals. In our experience int8 gives 1.8-2.5x throughput improvement on many models, but for safety-critical token predictions run the regression task set. Redwood Optimize can run diff-evals for you.
[04:45] Alex Chen: Also note kernel choice — some kernels are faster for int8, others for fp16. The runtime picks kernels based on model arch and sequence length distribution; you can pin kernel family for experiments.
[04:56] Michael Ross: About scheduler knobs again — are there automated policies, like maximize throughput subject to 95th < X?
[05:02] Priya Patel: We have autoscaling and policy routing, but not yet closed-loop automatic knob tuning in the field. We do provide recommendations and you can automate via our API to adjust max_batch_latency_ms or pool size based on SLO breaches. We're working on more automated tuners.
[05:18] Daniel Kim: Our network egress and KMS calls add jitter, anything we can do with VPC placement?
[05:24] Alex Chen: Keep KMS and your Redwood Private control plane in the same AZ if possible. Also colocate the inference pool and the ingress path — e.g., ensure pods have local NAT gateways so egress latency is minimal. For on-prem, make sure your HSM latency is profiled; sometimes a few dozen ms per key operation adds up.
[05:41] Sara Li: For our staging run, what's the recommended set of metrics to capture?
[05:45] Priya Patel: Capture per-request: total latency, queueing latency, decode time, KV cache hit/miss, batch size distribution, token count, GPU utilization, and 99/95/50 latencies. Also capture per-batch composition: how many sequences and their length distribution.
[05:58] Alex Chen: We'll send a benchmark script that emits realistic prompt distribution and records those fields back to a CSV.
[06:04] Michael Ross: Great. Can you give an example configuration you expect to perform well for us?
[06:08] Priya Patel: For your mix and 13B int8 on the current instance type, start with: max_batch_size=24, max_num_seqs=6, max_batch_latency_ms=15, per-route token_limit=200 for chat route. Keep a separate pool (or route) with max_batch_size=8 and no packing for the long-form generation.
[06:29] Daniel Kim: If we start there, what improvement should we expect?
[06:32] Priya Patel: Typically 30-60% better throughput and 10-30% lower 95th for small-chat traffic when switching from naive defaults to tuned packing and latency knobs. YMMV depending on real token distribution.
[06:44] Michael Ross: Any immediate pitfalls? I'm worried about oscillation when autoscaler scales pods and we keep seeing cache cold-starts.
[06:52] Alex Chen: For oscialltion reduce scale-to-zero aggressiveness and set a min-pool-size during morning hours. Also use smarter eviction — if throughput drops below threshold, spin up new pod but keep some warm pool so you don't hammer cache.
[07:06] Priya Patel: Another pitfall is over-aggressive packing with very long sequences — it increases memory pressure and can lead to OOM if not bounded by max_tokens and per-seq truncation. So always set both packing limits and hard token caps.
[07:20] Michael Ross: Understood. One more question on KV shard placement — is that configurable today?
[07:26] Priya Patel: Yes, on Redwood Dedicated/Private we expose shard affinity controls. You can route requests by user_id hash to maintain locality. On hosted there's less control but we do affinity heuristics.
[07:38] Daniel Kim: We also use SSO and need audit logs — does tuning affect logs?
[07:43] Alex Chen: No, observability is orthogonal — we retain token-level cost and latency breakdowns, and audit logs are configurable; tuning won't remove that data.
[07:51] Sara Li: Okay, let's talk follow-up scheduling at the end.
[07:55] Alex Chen: Sure, quick recap of recommended starting knobs: max_batch_latency_ms 10-25ms, max_batch_size 16-32 (or lower with packing), max_num_seqs 4-8 depending on memory, server-side per-route token limits. Pre-warm KV prefixes for top requests, keep min-pool-size during peaks.
[08:14] Michael Ross: Sounds good. We'll run the benchmark and share prompt distribution.
[08:18] Priya Patel: We'll share the tuning playbook and the benchmark script by tomorrow. Also include a sample config for EKS.
[08:25] Daniel Kim: Thanks all. A quick note — for our compliance team we may want to pilot in Private mode with KMS/HSM for keys, how different is the tuning there?
[08:34] Alex Chen: Tuning principles are the same; the difference is you get stronger affinity and local HSM latency to account for. We'll include a section in the playbook on on-prem/HSM considerations.
[08:45] Sara Li: Great. One last nit — our traffic sometimes sends a user metadata blob with each request, does Redwood strip/ignore it or does it affect batching?
[08:53] Priya Patel: Metadata doesn't change batching — only sequence tokens matter. But large metadata in the payload can increase network serialization time, so keep metadata separate or small.
[09:03] Michael Ross: Perfect. Let's wrap and confirm action items.
